sentences.text: Helicoprion possessed a skeleton made of cartilage, with only the jaw material being mineralized while the rest likely decayed rapidly.
Its body was streamlined and torpedo-shaped, featuring triangular pectoral fins, a single large dorsal fin without a spine, and a tall, forked tail.
The genus was first named in 1899 by Alexander Karpinsky based on fossils discovered in Russia and Australia.
The generic name Helicoprion translates to 'spiral saw', referring to its unique dental arrangement.
Helicoprion was likely an active, open-water predatory fish that used its tooth whorls, located in the lower jaw, to grasp and slice soft-bodied prey like cephalopods.

It was probably a bite feeder rather than a suction feeder, capturing prey with rapid jaw closures and sawing motions where front teeth snagged, middle teeth speared, and hind teeth punctured and pushed food into the throat.
The animal belongs to the genus Helicoprion, with the type species H. bessonowi and two other recognized species, H. davisii and H. ergassaminon, following a 2013 revision.
Taxonomically, it is placed in the extinct order Eugeneodontiformes within the clade Holocephali.
Fossils range from the Artinskian to the Roadian stages, indicating the animal lived during the Early to Middle Permian, approximately 290 to 270 million years ago.
Helicoprion was pelagic and had a cosmopolitan distribution, as fossils are found in marine deposits worldwide.
Eastman challenged Karpinsky's interpretation in 1902 by assigning the species to the genus Campyloprion, while Oliver Perry Hay later transferred it to Toxoprion in 1909.
It is debated whether Parahelicoprion is a distinct genus or a junior synonym, and relationships within the eugeneodont group remain unclear due to fragmentary fossil remains.
